analysis.title: Early Morning Reid - Macro Strategy
key_insights: DB US equity strategists upgraded US tech from neutral to positive over the weekend, reversing a move made three weeks ago. They say tech underperformed the market by 16% over those three weeks (tech -11%, rest of the index +6%). The sector sits at the bottom of a channel versus the index that it has bounced off 5 times in 2.5 years.

October review: Brent crude rose 13.6% on concerns over renewed US-Iran escalation, and European natural gas rose above €100/MWh for the first time since 2022. Treasury yields hit post-2002 highs early in the month but the asset class posted its best monthly return of 2026 (+2.3%). The Nasdaq fell 5.3%, its worst month since March 2025, on AI capex concerns. The STOXX 600 gained 2.0% and the equal-weighted S&P 500 gained 5.0%.
European credit and banks struggled in October as the OAT-Bund spread neared its 2011 peak. French sovereign stress was one of the month's themes alongside AI doubts and energy prices.

Tomorrow's US midterms decide control of Congress. Democrats are favoured to gain the three seats needed for a House majority. Polymarket puts the Democrats' chance of taking the Senate at 72.0% and Nate Silver at 75%. Results could take several days if margins are tight.

DB economists say the post-election lame-duck session may matter as much as the new Congress. Government funding expires December 11, and Republicans are likely to seek a reconciliation bill that could include additional defence spending and possibly address the debt limit.

Markets will watch the Iran conflict after the midterms. The concern is that energy prices become a less pressing political issue once the vote is over, allowing more aggressive action in and around Iran. Brent is down 3.47% this morning after Axios reported Trump favours giving diplomacy longer rather than imminent strikes, and S&P 500 futures (+0.49%) and Nasdaq 100 futures (+1.01%) have rebounded.

DB expects October payrolls of +55k (September +29k), private payrolls +55k (prior +46k), unemployment steady at 4.2%, average hourly earnings +0.3% MoM (prior +0.1%). Their payroll-based proxy for nominal compensation growth would ease a tenth to 4.1% YoY.

DB expects ISM manufacturing at 54.8 (prior 54.5) and ISM services at 55.1 (prior 54.9), ADP at +75k (prior +90k), and the University of Michigan preliminary sentiment index at 45.7 (prior 48.0). The prices paid components are flagged as worth watching.

The Fed left rates unchanged at last week's FOMC and Chair Warsh reiterated that further tightening is likely needed. DB economists think the labour data, barring downside surprises, will reinforce expectations of another hike at the December 9 meeting. Williams speaks Friday, and the Treasury quarterly refunding announcement is Wednesday.
Market-implied probabilities of a hike are 70.4% for the Riksbank (Wednesday), 95.6% for the BoE (Thursday, its first hike since 2023) and 4.4% for Norges Bank (Thursday).
DB economists expect the RBA to hold tomorrow even though the market prices an 82% chance of a hike.

China's official October manufacturing PMI fell to 49.3 from 50.1 (consensus 50.0). Production fell to 49.8 from 51.7 and new orders to 49.4 from 50.5, while high-tech manufacturing held at 51.3. Non-manufacturing PMI slipped to 49.7 from 50.2 (consensus 50.0), with construction weak and services flat at 50.0. The private manufacturing PMI matched expectations at 52.0 (September 52.1).

Asian equities rebounded this morning: KOSPI +2.77% led by SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, CSI 300 +0.89%, Shanghai Composite +0.97%, Hang Seng +0.72%. Kioxia fell over 15% in Tokyo after a Q3 forecast miss and is now just over 11,000 versus over 36,000 in late June, which DB cites as evidence of dispersion in the AI trade.
South Korea's S&P Global manufacturing PMI fell to 51.3 in October from 53.9, the lowest since February.

Last week the Philly semiconductor index went from over +8% on the week as of Wednesday to a fourth straight weekly decline (-0.84%) after a -7.20% drop on Friday. The Nasdaq fell 2.00% on the week and 2.86% on Friday, its worst day since June. The Mag-7 fell 2.24%, with Alphabet down 12.61% and Amazon down 3.08% after underwhelming results. The S&P 500 fell 0.57% (-1.82% Friday) while the equal-weighted index rose 0.80%.

Treasuries outperformed last week: 10-year yield fell 6.6bps to 4.93% and 2-year fell 9.4bps to 4.59%, both seven-week lows. Bunds, gilts and OATs also rallied. European IG spreads tightened 4bps and HY 12bps.

Brent ended last week at $117.64/bbl, close to its 2026 high, on US-Iran re-escalation worries. Gold fell 3.04% and silver 8.89% on the week to their lowest levels since last autumn. The Brazilian real fell 8.44% and the Israeli shekel 1.12% after their elections.

Earnings this week: Apple and Palantir today, AMD and Arista tomorrow, ARM, Qualcomm, McDonald's, Novo Nordisk and Uber Wednesday, Toyota, Sony, Deutsche Telekom, Rheinmetall and Nintendo Thursday, Moderna and Mitsubishi Heavy Friday.
